quote: How are you doing today? Got no form. I'm in got no form.
stewart_read: The rep's opening reference to 'the solar form you filled out online' is immediately disputed by the customer, and the rep never offers a specific detail (date, source, address confirmation beyond reading it back) to re-establish legitimacy before pivoting into the pitch.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep simply had no more specific lead data available, so there was nothing more to offer. This is plausible given the rep only had an address to cite.
coaching_implication: When a customer disputes the form, pause and confirm one more specific identifying detail before moving into the pitch — this is a reasonable practice suggestion, not a verbatim schema requirement, since Ion's script doesn't prescribe an exact recovery line for disputed lead legitimacy.

quote: It our neighbor on the street has it. And, you don't pay how much for the electric, but still he's paying for the for the solar energy panels and everything like that. He's losing money.
stewart_read: This is a textbook cost/value objection dressed as an anecdote. The schema's flip pattern (reframe the customer's own framing — 'what's expensive is not switching') is available here, but the rep instead argues logically point-by-point ('No. Not at all. I mean, it's replacing your current electric bill.'), which keeps the customer arguing rather than creating the pattern-interrupt the inversion move is designed to produce.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: the rep may be intentionally staying calm and factual rather than confrontational, judging the neighbor anecdote as a factual misunderstanding better solved with information than a rhetorical flip. But the customer's response pattern (restating the same complaint twice more) shows the factual approach didn't land.
coaching_implication: Coach the specific flip here: acknowledge the neighbor story, then redirect to the customer's own bill as the actual expense, rather than defending the mechanics of how solar offsets a bill in the abstract.

quote: They got panels all over the roof there and everything. And he still pays electric bill.
stewart_read: By the third repetition of the neighbor objection, the rep has an opening to pivot entirely away from defending solar mechanics and instead create curiosity about the customer's own numbers (e.g., 'let's just see what your specific numbers would look like'), but instead asks a clarifying question about the neighbor's system, keeping the conversation on someone else's situation rather than the prospect's own bill.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: the rep may have believed clarifying the neighbor's coverage percentage would resolve the misunderstanding factually. The follow-up question is reasonable on its face but does not redirect to the customer's own math, which is the higher-leverage move per the schema.
coaching_implication: When an objection repeats a third time, that is the signal to change tactics entirely — pivot to the customer's own bill/curiosity hook rather than re-engaging the same anecdote.

stewart_read: The customer gives a concrete, usable bill figure ($240/month) after nearly three minutes of objection handling — a real anchor point. The rep never gets the chance to use it because the very next line disqualifies the customer on utility provider.
coaching_implication: This bill figure is captured but the call ends before any flip is possible — flag this as a lost opportunity only in the sense that the DQ came a beat too fast to even acknowledge the number, not as a rep skill failure.

quote: Gotcha. So I actually know that we we don't work with Valley Electric anyway. So I'll just take you off my list here. I appreciate your time.
stewart_read: The call ends abruptly on a hard DQ with no summary, no explanation of why Valley Electric specifically disqualifies the lead, and no attempt to check if there's an alternate use for the contact (e.g., referral, future service-area expansion). This is a legitimate hard gate, but the close is bare procedurally.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: given the customer had already refused solar three times, the rep may have judged further engagement wasn't worth the time regardless of the DQ, making the fast exit efficient rather than sloppy.
coaching_implication: Even on a fast DQ, a one-line clean close ('Looks like we don't currently service your utility area, so I don't want to waste your time — thanks for chatting') gives the customer a clear, respectful reason rather than the abrupt 'take you off my list' phrasing, which can read as dismissive.

coaching_implication: Flag this as the second of three identical touches — the manager should see the full pattern (00:51 refusal, 01:09/01:19 neighbor anecdote, 02:19 restatement) as one continuous miss, not three isolated issues, to make the repetition visible in the replay.
